Mr. Speaker, when I completed the first part of my speech at five o'clock I was dealing with the extent and effect of the cuts in funding affecting scientific research in general and research in the field of medicine in particular. I want to put on record what the cuts announced in September mean to medical research in this country.
In the Department of National Health and Welfare the total science support cutback for 1978-79 amounts to $10.3 million. It includes $3 million for the professional training program which was used for the upgrading of health personnel and about which the minister spoke so glowingly, and $4.8 million in programs for research into the non-medical use of drugs. The use of drugs is increasing. The complexity of the drugs being taken is growing and the effect of drugs in such important aspects of life as mind control can probably be seen in the tragedy which occurred at Jonestown some days ago.
November 27, 1978

The amount of $2 million has been cut from the national health research and development program, besides $500,000 from the research budget of the Medical Research Council. We are talking about the kind of stop-go decisions which this government has been making over a period of almost ten years and which in the view of researchers, medical researchers in particular, constitute a disaster. Each time this sort of thing happens it is an indication, almost an order, for some of our youngest and best medical researchers to take off for the United States where they consistently spend not just ten times the amount on medical research one might expect, since the population there is ten times that of ours, but probably one hundred times what we spend. In other words, they spend $10 per capita on medical research for every $1 we spend here. The result is that the discoveries are made in the United States and we become captives of the American market.
Then the research budget of the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Gillespie) is $1.8 million; $1 million has been cut from the National Research Council and $500,000 from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council. The National Research Council has a worldwide reputation for the excellence of its work, but if this reputation is maintained no thanks will be due to the government. The effects of what the government has done and is doing will be seen not just this year or next year but in the decade and the generation to come.
It is an amazing set of decisions the government has made. In view of our high unemployment and poor balance of trade record, and the overwhelming evidence from other countries of the benefits of a strong research and development effort, these cutback proposals make no sense at all. Research is a labourintensive activity which employs people in each of our provinces and, dollar for dollar, yields high dividends by comparison with other work.
In his announcement last June the then minister of science and technology said that he was aiming in five years to spend 1.5 per cent of the gross national product on scientific research and development. More than half of that which other western countries are spending has already been cut in Canada in scientific research in the announcements I have already listed.
A particularly disturbing feature of the proposed federal cutbacks in research, health care and education programs is that now the responsibility for continuation of support for work in these areas could fall very heavily on the already financially beleaguered provinces. Although the established programs financing agreement requires the federal government to obtain provincial consent for any action that reduces or diminishes Ottawa's contribution, the announcement on September 8 shows that the Government of Canada intends substantially to reduce payments to these cost-shared programs, probably by cutting cash payments rather than through transfer of tax points.
The effect of any major federal withdrawal may be offset somewhat through equalization grants, but in the final analysis
Health Resources Fund Act
there is no guarantee that the less affluent provinces especially could afford to assume the high cost of funding research, health care and education on their own.
The minister suggested in her speech that since 85 per cent or 88 per cent of the money allocated under the legislation in 1966 had been used, the needs of the provinces had been met. Nothing could be further from the truth. In my own province there is approximately $8.5 million which has not been used, despite the fact that our largest teaching hospital, the Health Sciences Centre, urgently requires modification. That hospital is short of teaching staff, emergency care and laboratory care facilities. It is in need of advanced diagnostic laboratories and of upgrading in its child health facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Did you say the Seven Oaks Hospital?

I am talking about the Health Sciences Centre. The psychiatric facilities in that hospital are a disgrace. The minister may think that I have exaggerated the situation. The former head of medicine at the Health Sciences Centre, Dr. Reuben Cherniack, a nationally known researcher, left Winnipeg for the United States because of the lack of opportunity and facilities in that hospital. He is quoted in an article in the Winnipeg Tribune, July 5, 1978 as saying:
A chronic shortage of research facilities, coupled with a negative attitude toward research, has reduced the Health Sciences Centre to a second-rate community hospital and forced the University of Manitoba medical school downhill-
Further on in the same article he says:
-research uncovers new methods of approach, new methods of treating disease which are then applied to patients in the hospital.
But more important is these researchers developed labs that quickly became applicable to the patient. That isn't happening now.
The researchers are getting frustrated (by the attitude), their students are getting turned off. The future researcher is not going to be turned on.
A news story in the Winnipeg Free Press of last Saturday reports on a letter of protest that was sent to the minister of health in the Manitoba government, Mr. Sherman, by the former president of the Manitoba Medical Association, Dr. J. H. Crust, who protested vigorously about the fact that in the hospital in which he works, the Misericordia Hospital, seriously ill patients are denied beds because there are none available. In another story Dr. Crust talked of a patient of his who needed an operation and was left in the corridor in the emergency ward for 24 hours.
The story would be amusing if it were not so sad. The organized medical profession in Manitoba worked so hard to defeat the NDP government because they thought that it was unsympathetic to the medical profession and health care, only to find that the present Conservative government is no better.
The minister said today that the situation was not that bad in the field of medical research and tried to create the impression that the medical research community was relatively satisfied with the state of research and the support which it is getting from the federal government. I have a news clipping from the Ottawa Citizen dated October 18, 1978, which reports a speech the minister made at a meeting arranged by

an organization called Canadians for Health Research. It reads:
'I know you were hoping that I have been able to bring you an announcement that there would be increased funding made available and I wish I could have done that today, but regrettably I cannot do that'-
She stressed that while the $2 billion budget cutback hurt and meant a real 'tightening of the belt in government,' medical research would not be 'put on the back burner until our other economic difficulties go away'-
Further on the same article says:
"But the commitment that I want to make to you is that, even in a time of cutbacks and restraint, funding for medical research will be protected and will grow at least within the guidelines which the federal government has set to control its own growth."
The question is, do medical researchers accept the guidelines established by the government as being adequate? I suggest that they do not and that they have not for a long time. A letter written to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on March 1, 1976, by Dr. Victor Chernik, Professor and head of the Department of Pediatrics, and pediatrician-in-chief at the Children's Centre at the University of Manitoba, illustrates the current situation in medical research. It reads:
The level of funding for medical research in Canada on a per capita basis is approximately $2.00... while that in the United States is approximately ten times this rate. Thus, we are in danger of losing our best people, scientists who would compete very favourably in the U.S. funding arena.
In the last paragraph of his letter the doctor says:
In my own department there are several excellent investigators who have had to curtail excellent research programs in the diseases of children and several other young but very promising scientists who have not been able to get their programs off the ground because of serious lack of funding of the MRC. I submit that if the current policy of the Government of Canada is not altered medical research in the country will within the next three to four years be in serious jeopardy because of a lack of highly skilled and trained technical help, a major decline in the number of research trainees and the emigration of skilled scientists to areas which have a more stable funding base and are therefore more conducive to medical research.
The fears of Dr. Chernick have proven to be well founded because all the things he predicted have happened.
I have another article from the Winnipeg Tribune, dated April 28, 1977, which outlines the problems of medical research in my province. Manitoba is far from being the worst province in this area. This article reads:
What is lacking in this province, as in others, is money-money to attract high calibre people to Manitoba to perform research, teaching, and patient care functions, and to sponsor projects initiated by residents of the province.
It goes on to say:
Manitoba researchers reacted to the decision with alarm-
That is to the cutback at the time.
-noting that their purchasing power was cut by 35 to 40 per cent. Several research projects were scrapped and 38 research technicians in Manitoba lost their jobs.
There are probably another 28 who will lose their jobs this year. Let me bring the story up to the present. I have here a letter written to me on May 1 of this year from Dr. R. W. Hudson, secretary, research committee of the faculty of medicine of the University of Ottawa. In that letter he says in part:

The research committee of the faculty of medicine of the University of Ottawa feels impelled to make a public statement to the effect that:
1.	A crisis exists in medical and health related research in this country as a result of government funding policies.
2.	Long-term effects on medical research will, in turn, seriously affect health care delivery in Canada and the effect will be with us for many years to come.
3.	Over the last five years the government has failed to respond appropriately to representations by many groups from within the field of health care, as well as by those from outside.
It is clear that the present government must take full responsibility for the present crisis and for the consequences that follow.
Last but not least, I have a letter sent to me by Dr. Cinader from the Institute of Immunology, the school of graduate studies of the University of Toronto. He applied for a grant for a project entitled, "Geriatric changes of the immune system," and he received a reply from R. A. Heacock, director, contributions and awards division of the research programs directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare, which reads as follows:
As you have probably heard by now, the current series of expenditure cuts by the federal government will mean that the allotment of funds for the national health research and development program has been reduced by $2 million for the fiscal year 1979-80.
Having reviewed our budgetary commitments for the next fiscal year, it appears that in all probability no funds will be available to support any new projects and awards in 1979-80.
Dr. Cinader wrote to me. He is not complaining for himself because he is an established researcher who has access to other sources of funds, especially from the United States. He wrote to me on November 15 because he knows from past experience that I have been interested and involved in these discussions. His letter reads in part:
The recent decision that cuts of $2 million are to be made in external grants, given by National Health and Welfare (NHRDP), is a regrettable consequence of the current fiscal policies of the Canadian government. We are informed that the minister has decided to discontinue to consider newly proposed projects in 1978 and in the normal review period of 1979.
This will further increase the harmful long-term consequences of the scientific basis of our health services. When cuts are made, they must be carefully designed so as to protect the most valuable and original aspects of research, and must not occur at the expense of new progressive concepts. speakeroldname: Mr. Hal Herbert (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to address a few words to the House on this bill, but before I do so 1 want to make a few points of clarification regarding some of the remarks of the last speaker.
First of all, no submission for medical or hospital research has been refused by the department. Second, all agreements that have been signed will be honoured. At present, 85 per cent of the funds set up for this purpose have been utilized. It is obviously false to criticize this bill in an attempt to promote medical research.
Having said that, may I say a few words about the bill itself. A royal commission on health services, commonly known as the Hall commission, was established in the early 1960s at the urging of the Canadian Medical Association. The association, encouraged by the success of physician-sponsored service plans, felt that the "supplement not supplant" philosophy of public funding of medical care insurance for low income groups only would find support. However, after carefully conducting the most thorough and complete survey of the health situtation in Canada so far undertaken, the commission came out strongly in favour of a shared-cost program parallel to the hospital insurance program; in other words, a universal and government operated medicare program.
The medical care program which was implemented in 1968 was based on the 1964 recommendations of the royal commission on health services. It is important to look at some of the significant factors that led to its recommendations.
During the mid-1960s when the program was being considered, Canada was one of the few industrial nations without a national medical care insurance program. Although universally available plans existed in a few provinces, in most provinces there were Canadians who found it impossible to buy protection against the cost of medical care. In some cases this was due to ill health or age, with no insurance company willing
Health Resources Fund Act
to take the increased risk associated with issuing a policy. In other cases, individuals who were not members of an insurance group could not afford the higher premiums required for individual enrolment. It was only in those few provinces which embarked upon the governmental prepaid medical insurance plan, pioneered in Saskatchewan in 1962, that any resident who was not a member of an insurance group could with certainty buy comprehensive coverage without producing evidence of being a good risk, and without the possibility of being asked to pay a higher premium.
I should like to interject a very personal note at this point. I was in that position myself. Because of certain conditions and situations, I was the father of a family which was subject to sickness in the household day after day, week after week, month after month. Because I had not been enrolled previously in any assistance plan, it was impossible for me to obtain the necessary coverage. Debts accumulated, and every time a member of my family had to enter hospital, the debts increased. I found myself in an extraordinary situation. I was running out of any method by which to pay my bills. I had gone to the bank and finance companies. I was paying a tremendous interest rate of 18 per cent per annum on the money I was borrowing. I was in hock up to my eyebrows.
What does this have to do with the bill?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
I am pointing out how essential it was for the government to introduce a universal plan, so that persons experiencing extremely difficult financial conditions would be covered, despite the fact that no insurance company would touch cases similar to my own.
At the end of 1967, approximately 70 per cent of Canada's population was estimated to have some insurance protection against the cost of necessary medical care under voluntary plans. Eventually I was able to participate in one of those voluntary plans, but by then I had debts which I thought would never be repaid. An additional 4 per cent to 5 per cent were covered under a compulsory insurance plan in Saskatchewan, while others came under a variety of public programs for categorical assistance in receiving medical care. However, it should be noted that the Hall commission in 1964 reported that of those many Canadians who had private medical insurance, approximately 30 per cent had very inadequate coverage.
What benefits do we perceive from hospital insurance and medical care programs? The most obvious effect has been the removal of financial barriers to necessary medical, hospital and medical practitioner care for all residents of Canada. Again I should like to refer to my personal situation. Look at the embarrassment I faced when talking to a doctor who had performed a very expensive operation. I had to say to him, "Doctor, I have no way of paying your bill. I have borrowed to the limit." He said, "I will be sending you a bill. It will be a relatively small one. Pay it when you are able."
Ill health no longer means that families face crushing financial burdens related to costs, in addition to other misfor-

November 27, 1978
Health Resources Fund Act
tunes. Surely when one has sickness to contend with repeatedly, one should not also have to face financial concerns respecting the buying of one's daily bread.
The benefit of a medical care plan must be self-evident, but if proof is needed I should like to mention the 84 per cent to 88 per cent of the respondents in relatively recent Gallup polls who felt that they were receiving good value from health insurance, which topped the list of government finance services mentioned in the polls. The introduction of medical care programs meant that medical practice has become economically viable in any community with sufficient population to warrant a doctor, because of the virtual elimination of bad debts for medical practitioners. In itself this is a means of encouraging practice in areas where populations could not previously maintain an economically viable practice.
Once again, I should like to refer to a very personal experience. When my wife entered training school for nursing, she borrowed money from the provincial government, on the condition that either she repaid the loan or went to work in one of the areas where doctors would not go because the population was not particularly large, or because the population had no means of paying the doctor's bills. When my wife graduated from nursing school, she went to Baie Johan Beetz and spent a considerable amount of time there. She got to love the people of that community. As a newly graduated nurse, she did all the work one thinks of being performed by a doctor: delivery of babies, various kinds of minor surgery and extraction of teeth. These are the things one has to do when a community is completely cut off from the rest of the world for a period of several months, when there is no communication of any kind, other than that which can be dropped by aeroplane. There is no way of getting out and there is no way of getting in.
That is the type of medical service which was available to this community in the years prior to the introduction of a medical care program. The men and women who went into these areas certainly did not do so for financial gain. It was a tremendous strain on the individual concerned because most of them were young, enthusiastic, and had relatively little experience. They were called upon to perform some incredible tasks when helping with the problems of communities such as Baie Johan Beetz.
In addition to such general economic inducements resulting from the advent of the medical care program, the federal government contributed toward provincial monetary incentives to encourage physicians to establish in underserviced areas, such as the one I have mentioned. Obviously, those are areas where financial encouragement must be given in order to have the kind of medical service which is essential and necessary.
Every day we hear how bad things are in Canada, when really things could not be any better than they are at the present time compared to conditions in the rest of the world. We have more doctors per capita than any other country. We have extraordinary medical services. Any member of our population can go to hospital next week without having to worry about the bill. It is extraordinary that there should be objections to the kind of assistance which has meant that we

are able to send some of our surplus doctors into areas, where there has not been viable business for doctors in the past. In these small communities, not only was there no means by which a physician could be paid, but the gratitude of the people was often shown in some unusual fashion. For example, in my wife's case, she would receive jars of pickled fish, and all kinds of things which were quite precious in a community like that, as compensation for the services she performed.
As well as encouraging physicians to reside and practise away from metropolitan centres-who would not practise in a metropolitan centre today, and one of our problems is to get people away from these metropolitan centres-the medical care program has helped stimulate visiting specialist services for smaller communities. Once again, we talk about specialist services. Imagine being in an area where, not very long ago, it was not a question of getting a specialist's services but rather a question of whether you could get a doctor's services at all. This program brings these specialists to towns whose population is such, that they could not attract these specialists on a full-time basis. Of course, to the extent these services are going into areas not provided for previously, there is some associated increase in costs. But in a country as vast as ours, we feel dollars are well spent when they lessen disparity by bringing about better distribution of skilled human resources. We all know that one of the problems of the program-abuses, if you like-is that people in metropolitan areas are able to shop around, often from doctor to doctor, and draw on the expertise of the many specialists in those areas.
Canada has also experienced some dramatic improvements in certain health indicators. At the time our hospital insurance program came in, in the late 1950s, our infant mortality rate was more than 40 per cent higher than that of Australia, 30 per cent higher than that of England and Wales, and nearly 20 per cent higher than that of the United States. By the end of 1971, which was the first year that all provinces were in medicare for the full year, our infant mortality rate had dropped from 21.8 per 100,000 live births to 14.3, still equalling Australia's but surpassing that of the United Kingdom and New Zealand. In 1975 the Canadian rate was 11 per cent below that in the United States.

The maternal mortality rate on the eve of medicare was 27 per 100,000 live births. Incidentally, I was going to mention before I was so rudely interrupted by an hon. member opposite that one of the reasons for the mortality rate in days when we did not have a proper program was that in outlying communities more often than not-sometimes the percentage was as high as 75 per cent-the birth was not normal and required expertise. Often the people in those small communities were left with an inexperienced nurse who had to cope with some extraordinary problems.
The maternal mortality rate dropped a third by the end of 1971, and by 1976 was seven per 100,000. It is noted in some studies on the effects of implementing medicare that pregnant women were starting their prenatal care earlier than they had been doing before medicare. One presumes that, if prenatal care is of any value to the mother as well as to the baby, this earlier start of prenatal care may very well have had something to do with this marked drop in the maternal mortality rate.
Incidentally, I guess it goes without saying that if we can improve the facilities available to the mother at the time of birth, we are going to eliminate many of the problems encountered with all kinds of retardation in later life due to the inadequacy that used to exist in the facilities available at the time of birth.
I am not prepared to suggest that the improvements in maternal and infant mortality rates in the last ten years have been entirely due to medicare. However, it seems almost impossible to conceive that the tremendous change in the access to doctors, both physical and financial, since the introduction of medical insurance did not play some part.
With an increasing output from Canadian medical schools, Canada's doctor-population ratio is better than one in 600. We should be very proud of that. It has passed the target which the Hall commission despaired of reaching before 1991. As I mentioned a little earlier, I think we should sometimes talk about some of the good things in this country instead of always talking about the gloomy side.
All provinces have experienced a substantial improvement in their doctor-population ratios. Some changes have been especially gratifying. For example, the doctor-population ratio of Newfoundland, one of our less fortunate provinces economically, increased from one in 1,500 the year before medicare to almost one in 700, eight years after it joined medicare. As well as the improvement in the doctor supply over-all, more of the province's practitioners are settling in smaller communities. The increased supply of physicians and other health manpower relates to the significant impetus of the health resources fund established in 1966 which was complementary to the hospital insurance and medicare programs.

I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg North will pay attention to what I have to say. Today, in a crisis situation, the government is trying to give the Canadian people the impression that they are going to save a few dollars when in the long run it is actually going to cost millions.
I should like to summarize what the hon. member for Athabasca, this party's spokesman for health, so ably articulated earlier today. The federal government's health resources fund was created in 1966 to help provide money to meet the capital costs of constructing, renovating, acquiring and equipping health training and research facilities. For these purposes, $500 million was made available for use over a 15-year period. The fund was to pay up to 50 per cent of the cost, the rest to be provided by the provinces or some other source.
In December, 1967, things got off to a bad start. The minister of finance at that time, Mr. Mitchell Sharp, announced that he would seek to limit the total fund allocation
November 27, 1978

in the next fiscal year to $40 million. In fact, the total actually approved was $37.5 million. The same limitation was applied for the fiscal year 1969-70.
This change in rules in midstream caused chaos in the program ten years ago. In the first nine months of the fund, from July 31, 1966 to March 31, 1967, federal-provincial health officials agreed that $14.9 million should be given to various projects, but only $4.7 million was actually paid out by March 31, 1967, because of the federal government's intransigence. In the following fiscal year another $66.3 million was committed. Again because of the federal government's intransigence, the total payment was $32.6 million. That is how the fund got off the ground.
This on-again-off-again attitude of the federal government, aided and abetted by Treasury Board officials who cut into areas where they did not know what they were cutting, has created chaos when the object was to bring stability to the whole area. I say that Ottawa is slashing the health resources fund. I said this over ten years ago and I say it again today. This has had an alarming effect.
Let me talk for a few minutes about what the Castonguay report had to say indirectly about the province of Quebec vis-a-vis the health resources fund. The province of Quebec and the Castonguay commission typify only too well the Canadian scene vis-a-vis the delivery of medical and health care services, and indirectly the application of the health resources fund. Over 12 years ago the report concluded that regional planning was a number one priority in any progressive public medicare plan. Castonguay specifically recognized, as I said at the outset of my speech, that income supplementation through the hospital insurance plan and medicare was being voted into people's pockets for medical personnel and services that many times were not there, especially in low income and small town rural areas of this country.
The health resources fund not only had to address itself to this humanitarian difficulty but it had to address itself also to the cost spiral. At the centre of each region should be found a large health training centre with university affiliation, together with a large teaching hospital which should include all the highly specialized services, the report concluded. Decentralized from this large unit, often to be founded in smaller towns, cities and suburbs, the Castonguay commission recommended the establishment of general hospitals. I am now talking more particularly of the province of Quebec. These hospitals were to have over 200 beds for general surgery and specialized functions could be performed. Further decentralization as recommended by the Castonguay report should see the establishment of hospitals for the care of chronic diseases, old people's and nursing homes, ambulatory care centres, convalescent homes, health care clinics and so on.
When this bill passed the House, Ottawa obliged the provinces by allowing them to participate in a universal medicare plan, a hospital insurance plan, but we are voting again today meaningless sums to help make ready the facilities and person-
Health Resources Fund Act
nel needed under programs that were voted on over ten years ago. Quebec is no exception, Mr. Speaker. I address myself particularly to the minister right now when I say that regions all over Canada have embarked on medicare programs before services were initially prepared, and still the government is doing nothing in co-operation with the provinces to rectify the situation. I say that if this government persists in its attitude of pretending to save short-term dollars at the expense of longterm chaos, no one knows what the results will be.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have something to say to my colleague the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey).

The item under discussion today is the health resources fund. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) says that we should research all of the data so that we can make an intelligent decision. I propose to put before hon. members some of the facts which I believe will be helpful in making up their minds as to how they should vote on this particular bill. When the debate is over, if these facts do not agree I ask them to bring them up for debate so that we can look at them. Indeed, I have done my research on this bill.
In order better to understand the proposed amendment before us, I will refer to other programs having significant linkages to it in the past and currently. In the postwar period, significant impetus was given to the improvement of health care and services with the introduction in 1948 of the federal general health grants program to which the hon. member referred early in his speech. These grants had been referred to and described as "fundamental prerequisites of a nation-wide system of health insurance". This meant that the whole nation was going to be covered as equally as possible in a health scheme so that all Canadian citizens would have the best care and protection we could provide as a nation.
The objective has not changed. This bill will not be detrimental to the original concept of 1948. These grants provided financial support to the provinces for the development and expansion of public health services intended to prevent illness and disability, as well as to control tuberculosis, polio, measles and other communicable diseases; for the detection and early treatment of mental illness; for the improvement of health services for mothers and children; for the early detection and treatment of cancer; for the rehabilitation of the disabled; and finally, for research into problem areas. This is what we have been doing and what we are doing today. This work will in no way be detrimentally affected because of the bill before us.
Health Resources Fund Act
These grants also contributed to provincial health surveys of health services and resources, to the development of a standard accounting and reporting system for Canadian hospitals, and to improvements in diagnostic services. Through the hospital construction grant of 1948-1970, contributions in the amount of over $44 million were made to the provinces for the construction and upgrading of hospital and health facilities on the basis of $1,000 for each active treatment bed or its equivalent in diagnostic service areas, and $1,500 for each chronic or convalescent bed. Hon. members on the other side want to call this waste. I suggest it is not waste but a good investment for the benefit of all across Canada.
This grant assisted with costs of constructing space for more than 130,000 beds in active treatment, chronic convalescent, tuberculosis and mental hospitals; for more than 16,000 bassinets in newborn nurseries; for 24,300 beds in nurses' residences; for 900 beds in interns' residences; and for more than 8,300,000 square feet of floor areas for various hospital services available to both in patients and out-patients. Although not large in terms of the total cost of hospital construction, the grant provided an incentive which to no small degree assisted in providing new hospital beds and modernizing existing hospital buildings to meet the hospital bed deficit of 1948, the needs of a rapidly growing population in the 1950s and the increasing demand for hospital care following the introduction of hospital insurance in 1957-58.
The second step occurred in 1958, ten years later, with the implementation of the hospital insurance and diagnostic services program, under which the federal government shared in about half of the cost of provincial hospital insurance plans, which, of course, had to meet the minimum criteria of federal legislation.
With this implementation virtually all residents of Canada received more or less free hospital care, but given the inadequate level of private medical insurance coverage, there developed an incentive for both the doctor and the patient to use the hospital wherever possible. Canada had nearly seven insured hospital beds of various types per thousand of population throughout the sixties compared with approximately five per thousand in the United States; and, of course, with our program Canadians have greater financial access to those beds than the average citizen does in the United States.
So much for comparisons we always want to make with our neighbours to the south. So much for saying we are always the poor cousins. I suggest that the health care delivery system in Canada is second to none, not only on the North American continent, but the whole world over. As a matter of fact, Senator Kennedy is coming up here to get witnesses to testify before the United States senate committee, because he wants to implement a scheme there which is a good as ours. Here in Canada it is about time we told everybody how pleased we are with the things that we have, rather than always complaining about the things we do not have.
The net result was exactly what one would predict. Hospitals were used more. While admission rates per thousand are about the same as in the United States-between 162.1 and

November 27, 1978
Health Resources Fund Act
162.3 in 1964-the days of short-term hospital care are greater in number in Canada than in the United States-1,547, compared to 1,318 in 1974. In Canada, the average length of stay was approximately one and a half days greater-9.7 as compared with approximately 7.9 in the U.S. However, many short-term Canadian hospitals have long-term units, and if these are excluded, the Canadian figure becomes 1,389 days per 1,000 of population which is much closer to the U.S. figure.
During most of the 1960s, with this demand for the use of hospital beds, hospitals continued to be built in that time. We had the great hospital boom. Consequently, about 85 per cent of Canadian hospital beds are relatively modern and good for many years. When there are too many general hospital beds, regardless of the sophistication of budget review techniques, costs are difficult to control, especially when the supply is out of balance with care requirements. Many acute general hospitals cannot readily be converted to alternative uses, which would reduce the acute bed-population ratio more quickly.
In the Department of Veterans Affairs, many of the veterans presently in hospitals are not necessary acutely ill. They are there for temporary care, for long-term care and for rehabilitation. The veterans affairs department is in agreement with the provincial governments, that these men who served their country so well can be taken care of closer to their own homes and nearer to their friends and their families.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
However, most provinces are trying to lower the active treatment bed-to-population ratio down to something more in the order of four to four and a half beds per thousand of population, from the six or more that most provinces have. A great deal of emphasis is being placed on ambulatory care. In my own riding of St. Catharines in the last four years, we have opened four of these personal nursing homes, which provide personal care for the aged and the chronically ill. In this way we have helped to cut down a great deal the number of people who are using the beds in hospitals, so that those in greater need can get in and be treated properly.
The planning guidelines to cut general hospital beds vary. For example, in Ontario and New Brunswick the goals are set at about four beds per thousand of population in urban areas, and 4.5 beds per thousand of population in rural areas. The goal for Quebec is 3.2 beds per thousand of population, while British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Nova Scotia have set targets of 4.5 beds per thousand of population. Saskatchewan is a little bit higher with a goal of five beds per thousand of population.
It should be noted that in Newfoundland the bed standards depend upon the service performed, two beds per thousands of population, where there is no surgery performed, 2.5 beds where minor surgery is performed, 3.2 beds for regional hospitals and four beds per thousands of population for provincial referral hospitals. These statistics give an over-view of what is

going on right across Canada and enable us to compare how Canadians are being treated in hospitals; for example, how they are treated in British Columbia and how they are treated in New Brunswick.
These ratios reflect the practical recognition of several factors, including the current inventory facilities, the range of insured institutional alternatives-that is, special rehabilitation, chronic nursing homes and personal care beds-the extent of ambulatory programs and services, as well as the demographic factors such as age, sex, and distribution of population. Beds are currently being taken out of service through attrition or amalgamation of services, particularly maternity and obstetrical beds, because of the great population decline we have experienced in recent years. This population decline is also reflected in the schools, in the decline in the number of children attending, which in turn causes a decline in the needs of teachers and schools. In my opinion there will be very few new schools or new hospitals built in Canada in the next few years simply because we now have an adequate number of both. The adequate number of hospitals we now have enables us to deliver beds at an adequate level of health care, so that Canadians can be proud of what we have done, what we are doing and what we will be doing in the years ahead.
How is this being done? The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Andres) experienced the closing of a small hospital in his riding about a year ago.
Caused by the Tory government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
My colleague from New Brunswick says that it was a Conservative government that caused this. The Conservative government of the province said that restraints had to be carried out and they tell us they restrained selectively. I do not know what that means, but the member for Lincoln made it known that he would not stand for such a thing and subsequently the hospital was reopened. The hon. member knows now that the same level of health care is being delivered in his riding as it was prior to this cutback by a Tory government.
The role of the few general hospitals is being subjected to closer scrutiny than at any time in the past, and rightfully so. By continual review and analysis of actual health care needs, provinces are gradually and proportionately reducing the number of acute care beds and service relative to the population. Not only are we dealing here with healing people who are ill, but we are also dealing with preventive medicine, as touched upon earlier by the hon. member for Brome-Missis-quoi.
In the field of preventive medicine, Canada has made great strides. Recent unofficial figures for 1975 and 1976 show that the acute bed supply in Canada has decreased in absolute and relative terms from 128,000 in 1974 to 122,300 in 1976, or from 5.7 beds to 5.3 beds per thousand of population. The number of public hospitals in the last ten years has increased only slightly. The number of beds in public hospitals were 151,719 in 1975. With a beds-per-thousand ratio of 6.6,
November 27, 1978

including chronic, acute and convalescent beds, this has doubled the number of beds which existed some 25 years ago when the ratio was five.
I would like to deal briefly with the hospital insurance program, and also the utilization review. One of the most important spin-off benefits accruing from the hospital insurance program has been the tremendous bulk of statistics and data which can be used for planning and evaluation. The federal government has played a major role in standardization across the country of this data base. It has provided expertise for the provinces to set up a comprehensive data gathering and analysis system and the majority of provinces now have, because of this government, sophisticated computer application of these statistics. With this information they can measure themselves against any other province or city in Canada and determine whether they are delivering the health care which Canadians deserve.
Several volumes of hospital statistics for use by the hospital industry or other interested parties are now published on a regular basis yearly. At the hospital level the data are used for local administrative and planning purposes. At the provincial level the data are used, among other things, to make comparisons of the activities of similar hospitals, to assess the kinds of care, to estimate future costs for program planning, for research, evaluation, interpretation and ongoing administrative control.
The hon. minister at all times uses this data before she makes any decision like this for program planning and research. I would point out that in the field of research we provided in the last budget a great many incentives which will be good not only for our own citizens, but which can be used for the betterment of health care delivery for the citizens of the world. Canada was the country where insulin was discovered, which today is the greatest controller of diabetes, once considered a killer disease. It is now under control because of research that went on in Canada.
As I was saying, these data are also used, for example, as a control on utilization. Most provinces require long stay reports to be submitted on in-patients occupying a bed for longer than a specified period of time, generally between 15 to 30 days. Sophisticated computer programs have been devised in some provinces to compare the utilization of services in comparably sized hospitals. Again I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is very good because then you can see that your costs and your delivery system in a particular area are equal to those in another area, and if you are delivering not only quantity- which is what the hon. member on the other side was referring to-but quality in health care, with which we are involved here, it is quality which will not be compromised. This government would not think of compromising the quality of health care.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member wishes I had finished my comments. That is only because I am pointing out the good things while they on the other side are used to hearing gloom and doom. When anyone tells them the way things are, they clap two or three times and retire behind the curtains. Sometimes they are told to clap and wear blue suits.
Studies on the pattern of the flow of patients, particularly in respect of hospitalization, make facility planning and reorganization of services a more meaningful exercise. This is largely possible because of the wealth of data on patients and services which is being assembled continuously on computer tapes. All aspects of provincial health care, including hospital utilization, medical care utilization and supporting social programs, can be examined in the light of data now being acquired and put on computer tapes. These studies provide valuable information on the incidence of specific surgical procedures in relation to the age and sex composition of the beneficiaries, as well as data on the location and provision of service.
As a result, special committees are set up to determine whether the procedures are in fact necessary and, if so, whether they are carried out with the requisite quality considerations. For example, the rate of hysterectomies or tonsillectomies varies considerably between communities in relation to proximity to academic centres-
One more time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite wonder why I am laughing. It is because of some of the remarks that were made by hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski), the same hon. member who had the temerity today to table his football sweater. I am not sure of the number on the sweater. However, I do not want to get away from the subject. But this is why I laughed. I did not wish to be too serious about this. Now let me return to the more important things which we are here to discuss.
The cost of laboratory services for hospitalized patients and for ambulatory patients in government institutions, in hospitals or in private laboratories, can be obtained, analysed and evaluated.
Don't you wish you had a sweater to table!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
This brings me to the subject of utilization under the hospital insurance program. Utilization of Canadian hospitals, measured by per capita admissions, patient days and length of stay, historically has been higher than in the United States-there is no argument there. This was true for the period prior to the introduction of hospital insurance. On the whole, the margins were sustained during the 1958 to 1972 period. In more recent years, the differential between U.S. and Canadian hospital admissions has been narrowing and, in my opinion, will continue to do so. Canada's per capita admission rate is on the decline while the U.S. rate continues to increase.

November 27, 1978
Health Resources Fund Act
With recent curtailments in the acute bed supply, per capita admissions are expected to decline further.
The number of hospital admissions per 1,000 population increased during the 1960s but since then has stabilized or has tended to decline. Patient days per 1,000 of population followed a similar pattern, and in fact have declined more markedly in the 1970s. The average length of stay, which has increased up to 1968 and 1969, has since tended to become progressively shorter and now seems to have stabilized below the 1961 level.
Now I should like to deal with what is probably one of the more important aspects of this bill, namely the quality of care under the hospital insurance program. As viewed by the Hall commission, quality-
-depends primarily on the supply, availability, knowledge, skill and dedication of professionally qualified personnel, secondly on the facilities at their disposal, and thirdly, on the organization services.
The quality of health care in Canada, as measured by these standards, has certainly been improved as a direct consequence of the health insurance program and related programs such as the health resources fund and professional training grants.
The supply of suitably qualified and trained health manpower increased significantly in the early stages of the hospital insurance program, with the funding available to teaching facilities and hospital nursing schools under the program, as well as the increased employment opportunities during the initial period of growth. Under the legislation, provinces were required to make arrangements so as to ensure that adequate standards were maintained in hospitals, including licensing and inspection. What good is it if you set up standards in hospitals, but you have no way of finding out what the quality of standards is in those hospitals?
The tradition of voluntary accreditation has been maintained in Canada through the Canadian Council on Hospital Accreditation which regularly surveys hospitals and related facilities and whose activities closely parallel those of the American Council on Hospital Accreditation. The accreditation program is actually financially supported by the provinces which recognize surveyor fees as an eligible cost.
All provincial hospital insurance plans have provisions for peer review for hospital care, that is, tissue committees, utilization, and length of stay committees. Peer review mechanisms also exist under the provincial medical care insurance plans in respect of services claimed by medical practitioners for inpatient, out-patient and non-hospital care.
While the approach and application of peer review procedures vary somewhat from province to province, the fact that collated utilization data are available in respect of virtually the total population of each province, contributes to more meaningful peer review. Generally speaking, each provincial plan requires standardized record and accounting procedures, including claims for the services of medical practitioners, so that a fair degree of interprovincial standardization has evolved in these matters.

The organization of health services likewise has been influenced by the programs, especially after the implementation of the Medical Care Act which set the stage for more integrated planning and operation of health care facilities and services. Progressive patient care, unimpeded by financial barriers, became much more feasible, as did regionalization of health services once basic diagnostic and therapeutic services-that is, hospital in-patient, out-patient, physician care, public and private laboratory, radiology, etc.-became insured. So it would be wrong to suggest that health care would in any way be diminished or jeopardized.
The minister has discussed this bill with us in caucus many times. There have been innumerable committees from which she has gleaned information from her colleagues in the House. I am sure the hon. minister, as so many of us, welcomed the interventions of hon. members opposite; but instead of forever putting before us the negative aspect of things, perhaps they could point out some of the good things which have been done and are being done for Canadians.
In no small part these are due to the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has gone to great pains to see to it that not only the quantity of care is being maintained as much as possible in this time of restraint, but that the quality with which patients are treated in hospitals in no way can be affected detrimentally.
In the long run, the bill will be beneficial to all Canadian citizens. Also it will be beneficial in the short run, in times of restraint. I urge hon. members to vote for the bill now that some facts have been put before them, now they can judge for themselves and see the good things we are attempting to do in order to provide the health care which has existed in the past and will continue in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have listened with interest and some measure of consternation to the words of the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Parent). I am reminded of a speech which was given to a group of uneducated people in the southern United States during a political campaign a number of years ago. The speaker was attempting to bring about the defeat of the other candidate and he said, "You know that this man who seeks to represent you is a pragmatist. Worse still, he graduated summa cum laude, and when he got to university, he was a Phi Beta Kappa". He threw these words at the audience and astounded them to the extent that they thought the other candidate was some kind of a creature from Mars. By his choice of words and the inflection in his voice, he confounded and confused his audience and they bought what he said.
This is the type of game the hon. member for St. Catharines is attempting to play. I cannot speak for his side, but I can for mine. The educational level on my side is such that we are not prepared to grab that kind of garbage. The hon. member did not say that it was his government which was responsible for the discovery of insulin and for the support of the discoverers of insulin, but he implied it by the tone and inflection of his
November 27, 1978

voice. Then he went on to poke fun at the Conservative whip. He was not really poking fun at the Conservative whip. He was attempting to cover up what he thought was something humorous, because he does not know the difference between a tonsillectomy and a hysterectomy. I would be pleased to demonstrate that to him at any time.
I saw the man launch into full flight. He said, "How blessed we are". He sounded like Oral Roberts. According to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the enemies of the government are opposition members and the press. Do the enemies and the people of Canada consider that they are blessed by the government? They are not; they are cursed by the government. They will find out just how cursed they are when the government has the guts to pull the pin and call an election.
I listened to the astute observations of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). He is capable and quite facile at distortion. He likes to pick at things, and he picked today. He talked about the Tories preaching restraint on the one hand, and wanting to bring in the program in its full bloom on the other. He spoke out of both sides of his mouth. He knows full well that there are programs of value which must be continued. Certainly the Auditor General described the programs and policies of waste which can be removed.
The other evening I had the opportunity to watch television at which time the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) was being interviewed. I could not help thinking then that for perhaps the first time in a long while we have a dedicated and sincere minister, and I have not changed my views in that regard. Frankly, if the minister could have her own way she would not contemplate for a minute the kind of bill which she introduced. The minister has a better appreciation of the social needs in Canada than that.
The Prime Minister went to Bonn, and he sailed the lake with his counterpart in West Germany. He went to Morocco, twiddled his toes in the sand and suffered a fit of sunstroke. In that blush of sunstroke, he returned to Canada and went on national television. He confused Canadians and confounded his cabinet. After it was all over and the debris had settled, we have the benefits which supposedly are being reaped by Canadians because of so-called restraint. The big free spenders suddenly realized the error of their ways. But they have cut holus-bolus. They have amputated without consultation with the patient, without the benefit of anaesthetic. I suppose I do not have to ask the classic question: How can the minister in conscience implement this bill without first consulting with the provinces? But I would be astounded if the government did anything else.

subtopic: FORESTRY-DECISION NOT TO CLOSE PETAWAWA RESEARCH STATION
FORESTRY-DECISION NOT TO CLOSE PETAWAWA RESEARCH STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 14 and on other occasions the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand), in reply to questions concerning the amalgamation of the Forest Management Institute and the Forest Fire Research Institute in Ottawa with the Petawa-wa Forest Research Institute, indicated that the proposed amalgamation would result in considerable savings in administrative costs, and in his words would be good for forest services in general. He failed to say what it would cost in human terms, and said even less in terms of the loss of benefit to the forest industry in Canada.
I should like to put the picture into perspective. The minister spoke about the federal research arm of the industry which contributes approximately $6 billion to Canada's favourable balance of trade. This is part of the federal research arm of the industry which contributes something like $1 billion to the federal treasury and another $500 million to provincial treasuries. What are they slicing off? They are slicing $5.3 million from the budget.
What does the Canadian forestry service research cost in all? What does it cost when you consider the contribution it makes to the Canadian economy? I have made a rough calculation and it is something of the order of three-quarters of 1 per cent of the contribution to the export trade balance alone. I have made an attempt to find the figures in respect of federal contribution toward forestry research as a percentage of what the Canadian forest industry makes to the Canadian economy as a whole in terms of forest products, lumber, paper and employment, and I would suggest that the contribution there in those terms would be something of the order of .00 per cent.
Under this government, with the decrees after dark on August 1 on the road back from Bonn about which we heard just a few minutes ago, the Canadian forestry service finds itself in trouble, whatever the minister says. Why is the

November 27, 1978
Adjournment Debate
minister not prepared to wait, before following through with these cuts announced in August, until he has had the advice which he has sought, and which was due in June, from the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, or until a task force has been put together to come up with recommendations on the future of the Canadian forestry service?
The minister has responded to other questions on the future of the Canadian forestry service and has allowed it to be believed that the Canadian forestry service is in good shape and will have no trouble whatever surviving the cuts that will be imposed on it. Does the minister know that he is in danger of losing the director of the institute, one of the senior scientists, the entire professional staff of the forest appraisal and remote sensor programs, all experts in fields in which Canada has led the world for 50 years, as well as some of the best technical support staff? Is this a service that is in good shape and will be in good shape after these cuts take place?
The minister has also led us to believe by his replies that the privatization scheme which he has in mind, and about which he is not at all clear-because he talked about Crown corporations on the one hand, and then he dropped that and talked about privatization-has been warmly received by the forest industry. That is what he has led us to believe.
In support of that claim the minister has stated that the chief executive officer of Crown Zellerbach, Mr. Rogers, and chairman of the Canadian Forestry Advisory Council, indicated his support for the proposal for privatization, and particularly in respect of the proposals for the forest products laboratories in the west and in the east. The truth of the matter is that the industry is not so warmly supportive of this notion as the minister would lead us to believe.
What the forest industry has done, in fact, through the Canadian Forestry Advisory Council, which incidentally had not met for three years until brought together in a panic by the minister about a month or two months ago in order to get some advice on this problem, was ask for bridging funds and for a bridging time so that the labs could be properly worked into the system. They could not accept April 1 as a date that is meaningful in terms of closing down, as has been proposed, or privatization.
I am sure when the parliamentary secretary replies he will ask where else the cuts could be made, and that is a most important question. I have suggested there are nodes of interface between the policy end of the operation by the government and the sharp end of implementation in the field. There are too many of these intervening nodes of administrative interface-that is the buzz word these days, as euphemism for roadblocks-between the government and the field operations. The Department of Supply and Services has to be brought in to negotiate contracts. The Auditor General recently warned us what that means in terms of cost and overruns.
There is a plethora of regional offices which have not been operational but which have been asked to recommend cuts.

The minister said he has been advised by his officials but those officials are in the administrative field, not in the research field, and so do not know the value of the work being done. The administrative section is obviously not making recommendations for cuts in their own functions but have recommended cuts in the laboratories and the research stations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Donald Wood (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: FORESTRY-DECISION NOT TO CLOSE PETAWAWA RESEARCH STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has become apparent to me in the last little while that members of the House, and more particularly the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), are now fully realizing the importance of the forestry industry to Canada. Canada has always been known as a forest nation, and with the vast resources of its many provinces that will not change. In recent years there has been much diversification and industrialization in the forests, but that has really only gone to prove one thing-its limitless potential for the continued well-being of Canada.
One of the areas that has received more attention in the past few years is tree improvement and the intensification of forest management in general. Research has done wonders in the forestry industry, not only for the processing but more particularly as it relates to tree species and genetics. As a result of genetics, some of the new species can produce up to 50 per cent more wood than the older species in a given period of time. That is only a beginning and improvement in genetics will result in improvement in wood production.
This tree improvement research constitutes a major element of the Canadian forestry service research program. It is very important for the hon. member to fully realize and understand that the Canadian forestry service is much more than and plays a much larger role than mere research. It is responsible for the co-ordination of all federal policies which have anything to do with forestry. It must disseminate forestry statistics as they relate to the industry and it is very much involved in international activities and many other functions.
By far the largest part of these non-research activities falls to the headquarters of the Canadian forestry service. These offices are now staffed at the minimum level necessary and I am sure-at least I hope-that the hon. member would not want it to be otherwise.
I want to assure the hon. member that policy and economic studies will play a stronger role in the Canadian forestry service program in years to come. It is very important to keep all this in its proper perspective so that what the consolidation of the programs has meant and will mean to forestry in the future can be fully understood.
The consolidation of the Forest Management Institute and the Forest Fire Research Institute with the Petawawa forest experimental station will result in a strong, broadly based national research program. At the same time, substantial savings can be made in administrative costs. Again I say to the hon. member that I hope he is prepared to support savings and efficiencies as they relate to government spending.
