subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA-STATUS INDIANS
LABOUR CONDITIONS-UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA-STATUS INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recent changes in the unemployment insurance boundaries have combined northern regions of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta into one economic region. As a result the unemployment rate in northern Manitoba, which is the Churchill constituency, has dropped from 26 per cent to 4.6.
As you are no doubt aware, sir, the rate of unemployment in a region determines the length of work time needed to draw benefits and the length of time claimants can draw benefits. The more than 20 per cent drop in the unemployment rate in northern Manitoba means residents will now have to work 14 weeks instead of the former ten weeks required to claim benefits.
Contributing to this reduced unemployment rate is the fact that unemployed status Indians are not taken into account in Statistics Canada labour force figures. My question is: Why are status Indians not included in those statistics? Status Indians are part of the program; they pay into it, and they derive benefits from it. But now, because they are not included in the statistics of the unemployed, the qualifying period for unemployment insurance is longer and the re-entry period is extended to 20 weeks. This is a marked discrimination against Indian people. They are being treated as second class citizens and do not even rate Canada's statistics.
For the two years Canada Works has been in operation, the Churchill riding has received some of the highest grants for all of Canada. It is clear from the Statistics Canada figures used by Canada Works co-ordinators that northern Manitoba has a high percentage of people without work, and there are few jobs available.
Statistics Canada figures state that our labour force is nearly 35,000 in the Churchill constituency and that of these over 9,000 people are unemployed. More than half of the unemployed population, or 5,365, are status Indians. The Department of Indian Affairs puts the number of unemployed status Indians even higher at 7,993.
Regardless of the variations in figures, it is clear estimates exist that are at least semi-accurate. If the government can pinpoint our need for Canada Works dollars, surely it cannot turn a blind eye to the many status Indians who are unemployed and require unemployment insurance benefits.
The deputy minister of employment and immigration tried to tell me in committee on Wednesday that present survey measures are meaningless in assessing unemployment rates for status Indians on reserves, and that to devise alternate methods would involve substantial time and personnel resources. This is reprehensible. We are talking about people, the first people of Canada, being arbitrarily excluded from a government program to which they contribute, and in effect penalized because they are not part of the damned statistics.
The deputy minister of Indian affairs informed me Thursday there have been no discussions between the two depart-
Adjournment Debate
ments of Indian affairs and employment and immigration regarding the present distortion of the unemployment rate of the northern communities. When will this government deem this matter important enough to do something about it?
Will the concerned departments consider accepting figures from the department of Indian affairs for the number of unemployed status Indians on reserves? Or, alternately, will they accept a band council resolution certified by the chief and council as to the number of unemployed?
It is time this government took some action instead of having me run around to the different departments-employment and immigration, Indian affairs, and industry, trade and commerce, which is responsible for Statistics Canada-to change this contradictory and discriminatory policy. I want a firm commitment now that measures will be taken to ensure status Indians are included in the unemployment statistics of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Frank Maine (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA-STATUS INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Unemployment Insurance Act as amended by Bill C-27 requires the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission to use rates of unemployment produced by Statistics Canada for the purpose of determining eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits. Status Indians on reserves are not included in the rates of unemployment produced by Statistics Canada. Therefore, unemployed status Indians on reserves are not included in the rate of unemployment for the 48 regions.
As the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) has noted in committee, this is a problem with the unemployment rate provided by Statistics Canada, especially in northern Canada. Officials of the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission have been and will continue to be in contact with Statistics Canada to determine what can be done to rectify this situation.
I think it is fair to add that, based on official discussions held so far, it would not be an easy matter to adapt the traditional labour force survey to the particular conditions on reserves in which concepts of labour force employment and unemployment are different from those concepts when applied to the vast majority of the working population in urban centres. Indeed our advice from the bureau is that considerable time and resources would be required to come to grips effectively with the problem.
Nevertheless, we realize it is important that something be done, and we are therefore proposing to contact immediately the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to determine what action they, the bureau, and the commission might take to produce acceptable measures of unemployment statistics for status Indians on reserves, and gradually improve these over the years.
Hon. members will, of course, be aware that in the allocation of funds for the Canada Works program, labour surplus rates are calculated for Indians on reserves. These, we have to

November 27, 1978
Adjournment Debate
admit, are rough and ready estimates and are not produced by Statistics Canada. As a result, they could not be used for the purposes of the unemployment insurance program. Thus, it will be important for us to pursue immediately the course of action which I have outlined, that is to say, co-operative discussions between the commission, the bureau and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, to determine the most practical and acceptable means of resolving the problem.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-FEASIBILITY STUDY ON COAL MINE IN DONKIN, NOVA SCOTIA
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-FEASIBILITY STUDY ON COAL MINE IN DONKIN, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, further to my questions of November 15 when the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) was unavoidably absent, I should like to have the answers from his parliamentary secretary this evening.
Since the first phase of the feasibility study on the Donkin Mine has been finished, would it be possible to get a 12 to 20 page summary for myself and other interested members from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion standing committee? I realize that the report would be more than one volume and would be technical in detail, but I would be very interested in getting a resume.
As I indicated in my questions, the more important second phase that involves the economic feasibility of the prospects for the new mine should be soon ready. It was indicated to me by a top Devco official last August that they expect the second phase to be finished by March or April before it goes to the Treasury Board. Can the parliamentary secretary to the minister confirm this or give us a more accurate date for when this second phase of the study will be finished?
This, of course, involves, among other things, whether the decision is going to be to build a mine that will have an annual production of a million, two million or four million productive capacity. It goes without saying, Mr. Speaker, that this is extremely important to an area with such high unemployment.
The employment selection officer for the Cape Breton Development Corporation informed me that as of October 1, 1978 there are 1,850 applications from Glace Bay for general employment in Devco. There are another 2,000 from New Waterford. The total for the whole of the Cape Breton area was estimated as of October 1 to be 4,900.
One can see how critical this mine at Donkin is to the future of the area from an employment point of view; it would have spin-off effects which would make for at least another 1.5 jobs per worker in the rest of that economy. It also indicates the prime need to go ahead with the modernization of the Sydney Steel plant so as to avoid even more desperate levels of unemployment in the area. Similarly, it becomes urgent to press on with the operations in Prince Mine to meet the employment objectives which were mentioned when the mine was first started.

I referred to the steel industry in my remarks tonight because the future of the biggest employer in the Glace Bay area, mine No. 26 with its low sulphur and premium coking coal qualities, depends in part for its success on the Sydney Steel operation. One of the major concerns I heard expressed recently during my visit to the constituency is that the coal cleaning plant so vital to a reconstructed coal industry is still experiencing serious production problems.
I am told that in the last month there have been vast improvements in the operation of the plant, but as I mentioned in my question there are rumours that, because of its over-all failure to fulfil the expected potential, we may not be able to fill some of the coking coal requirements contracted for with such users of coke and coal as the Steel Company of Canada and Dofasco. If there is any truth to this it could be a serious blow to our prospects, because everyone with a knowledge of the industry knows that there is on average a $10 per ton premium at least for coking coal as against coal for use in generating thermal power. The prepared blends of coal from No. 26 with lingan coal make for an excellent metallurgical coking coal.
I ask the parliamentary secretary to provide answers to these questions which are bothering me.

speakeroldname: Mr. Donald Wood (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-FEASIBILITY STUDY ON COAL MINE IN DONKIN, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to reply to the hon. member; I only hope 1 shall have time in which to fully answer his questions.
The Donkin Mine feasibility study was originally scheduled to be carried out in two stages. Phase one was scheduled to begin in May 1978 with a'report which would compare the economics of several project configurations using cost estimates and assumptions regarding marketability and the like. If phase one gave indications that the mine would be financially viable, phase two would be undertaken to provide definitive cost and performance figures which would be presented to the Government of Canada with a request for the necessary funds to develop the mine.
Unfortunately, it was not possible to prepare the phase one report by October 6 because of delays in getting information from the offshore bore holes and the seismic surveys, information which was necessary to determine the size, extent and quality of the coal seams which would be mined during the next 30 years or so.
On October 11, 1978, a preliminary verbal report was presented to Devco management. This was followed on November 20 by a second verbal report which showed that several mine layouts would be economically viable. The report also indicated there were additional possible mine layouts which should also be studied to determine which would provide the greatest economic benefit.
In view of the delays experienced to date and the importance of maintaining the final date of February 28, 1979, the date by which phase two was to be completed, it was decided to dispense with the preparation of a formal report marking the end of phase one and to proceed directly with the work
November 27, 1978

required to complete phase two. This work is presently being done and the study is now on schedule.
The Cape Breton Development Corporation has not presented the first phase of the feasibility study to the minister. Verbal discussions were held with Devco management. The study is scheduled to be completed by the end of February, 1979.
Our metallurgical coal production has grown from approximately 417,000 tons in 1976 to 1.2 million tons in 1977. At the present time our production rate is running about 1.5 million
Adjournment Debate
tons. In the current year production rates have continued to improve, and had it not been for a short strike and operating difficulties in the early part of 1977, the full deliveries of coal would have been supplied to our Great Lakes customers.
